Thank you for the shawl. I'm wearing it right now in the hostel, and it still smells of your almirah.

I want to answer what you said on the phone on Sunday, because I just said "ji, ji" and then cried a bit after.

Kiran

Yamini, I see you've written "SHOULD WORK HARDER" on your monitor in red. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age at this same office.

One day my old boss, Mrs D'Costa, read it over my shoulder. She said, "Who wants to work for someone who shouts at them all day? Not even you."

So I changed one line. "I'd like to be more productive. Today: finish the Kolhapur file before tea."

It sounds silly. But I finished the file. And the next day I wrote another small one.

So maybe, Yamini, take off the red note. Try "I'd like to" and one thing.

qa.a: "I'd like to" invited rather than ordered, and the one concrete step before tea was easy to start. Finishing it lowered the guilt and led to another step the next day.

The construction next door started at eight every morning, drilling through the wall of Sonali's one-room flat in Indore. She was a freelance translator with three pending jobs and a head that kept saying: You should be more productive. You should have finished these yesterday.

By noon on Monday she had done nothing but feel guilty and sweep the drill dust off her desk twice.

Saurabh, her husband, came home for lunch and found her staring at a blank screen. "Bad day?"

"I should be faster. I should be better at this."

He handed her a sticky note. "Try another word."

She thought, then wrote: "I'd like to be more productive. Next step: translate one page before the drilling stops at two."

With earplugs in and the note stuck on the laptop, she did one page. Then, while it was still quiet, half of another.

It wasn't three jobs. But it was a start, and the guilt was quieter than the drill.

qa.a: Swapping "I should" for "I'd like to" and naming one step, one page before two. The kinder wording plus a clear, small target made action easier than guilt.

qa.a: Saurabh probably saw she was stuck, not lazy, and that the shoulds weren't helping. Offering a sticky note instead of advice let her find her own wording.

Rekha, eight, slammed the storybook shut on the bed.

"I'm dumb, Charu Mausi. I'm not reading anymore."

"Dumb? Who says?"

"Hmm. Yesterday who read me the recipe for halwa?"

"And who read the bus number from far away when I couldn't?"

"That's numbers."

"So you can read short things and numbers. Is that dumb?"

Rekha folded her arms. "It's long pages. Long pages hate me."

"Ah. So it's not 'dumb'. It's 'long pages are slow for me'. That's a different problem. Slow things get faster with practice."

"No, they don't."

"Let's check. One page tonight. I'll time you. Then same page on Friday."

I'm Aadhya and I'm eleven now. When I was eight, I thought I was lazy and dumb, because reading took me forever. The others finished the chapter and I was still on the first page, sounding words in my head.

So I stopped. If I was dumb, why try? I hid the reader in my school bag and said I'd forgotten it.

My friend Ira didn't believe it. One day she brought comics to my house. "Read me the bubbles," she said. "Only the bubbles." The bubbles were short, so I could. We read the whole comic. It took ages, but we laughed a lot.

We did that every Saturday. Slowly, my eyes got faster.

Now I know I wasn't dumb or lazy. I was just slow at reading, and slow can be practised. I still read slower than Ira. But I read.

At Tai's wedding lunch today, Mama said it again, laughing: "Tushar? He's our family's failure. Dropped engineering, now works in a print shop." Everyone laughed. I laughed too.

Funny thing is, I've started acting like it. I don't apply for anything. I don't answer when uncles ask about plans. If I'm the failure, why try? The word sits on me like a shirt I didn't choose.

But this evening at the shop something happened. Ganga-mausi, who owns it, was checking the wedding cards I'd set. She held one up to the light. "Tushar, you fixed the spacing on the Marathi lines without me telling you. You have an eye. Have you thought of learning design properly?"

Nobody has ever said "you have an eye" to me.

I walked home the long way. Maybe "failure" isn't all of it. Maybe I'll look up that design course. Just look.

Manjula, you asked what happened with the parents' meeting. Okay, here's the honest version.

I'm Devika, I teach Class 4, and on Friday I completely forgot that I'd scheduled Arjun's parents for 4 p.m. They waited twenty minutes in the corridor. I was at the market buying vegetables.

When the head teacher called, "Devika ma'am, they're still waiting," my first thought was: You're useless. You can't even keep a diary. What kind of teacher are you?

But I'd been practising something. So on the way back I said, out loud in the auto: "I forgot a meeting. That was irresponsible. I feel bad because they took time off work." That's different from "I'm useless." One is about Friday. The other is about my whole life.

I called them that evening, apologised, and offered Monday at 8 before school. And I put an alarm in my phone for every meeting now.

I still feel bad. But I also still feel like a decent teacher.

qa.q: Where was Devika when the parents were waiting?
qa.a: Devika was at the market buying vegetables.

qa.a: "I'm useless" is about her whole life and identity, while "I forgot a meeting" is about one Friday. Naming the act lets her feel bad without losing her sense of being a decent teacher.

qa.a: She called the parents that evening, apologised, offered Monday at 8, and set alarms for every meeting. Owning the mistake led to fixing it, which self-attack wouldn't have.

qa.a: They may still be a bit annoyed about the wasted time, but the quick apology and new slot probably reassure them. It shows Devika takes their time seriously.

grounding: A young teacher describes forgetting a parents' meeting as an irresponsible act rather than proof she is useless, keeping responsibility and self-respect.

I'm Vikas, and I've volunteered with Sunaina at the Saturday reading club for a year.

Last week she forgot the planning call with the library. The rest of us sat on the call for fifteen minutes, then the librarian left. I was annoyed, honestly.

On Monday, Sunaina messaged the group. I expected either nothing or a long "I'm so useless, I'm the worst" message, like people usually send. Instead she wrote: "I forgot Saturday's call. That was irresponsible of me, and I'm sorry you all waited. I've called the librarian and fixed a new time: Wednesday, 6 p.m. I've set two reminders."

That was it. No drama, no hiding.

I don't know what she felt inside. Maybe she beat herself up privately. But what I saw was someone owning a mistake without making herself into the mistake.

I found I respected her more after it than before. I've started trying to write my own apologies that way.

qa.q: What new time did Sunaina fix with the librarian?
qa.a: Wednesday, 6 p.m.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's message suggest about how she was thinking about the mistake?
qa.a: It suggests she saw the forgetting as something she did, not who she is, so she could own it and fix it without spiralling. The calm tone points to self-respect alongside regret.

qa.q: What made Sunaina's apology work, and what could others copy?
qa.a: It named the act, said how it affected people, apologised, and gave a fix and reminders. Others could copy that clear structure instead of calling themselves useless.

qa.q: How did Sunaina's apology change the way Vikas felt?
qa.a: Vikas was annoyed at first, but ended up respecting her more than before. Seeing a mistake handled without drama made Vikas want to apologise the same way.

grounding: A volunteer watches a young woman describe forgetting a meeting as an irresponsible act, not proof she is useless, and admires her for it.

At the residential school in Shillong, lunch in the dining hall was usually loud at their table. Today Sonali just pushed rice around her plate and looked out of the window.

Mehak's stomach tightened. What did I do? She went through the morning. She'd borrowed Sonali's geometry box without asking. She'd laughed at Sonali's wrong answer in chemistry. Last night she'd switched off the dorm light while Sonali was still reading.

Sonali looked confused. "What? No. My grandmother's not well and I can't go home till the holidays. I've been thinking about her all day."

Mehak sat back. None of the list had anything to do with it.

The inter-college case competition was held in the seminar hall of the polytechnic in Bhopal. Divyansh's team of five came fourth out of six.

The judges' feedback sheet had six lines. "Strong analysis. Weak time management; ran four minutes over. Financial slide added late and not rehearsed. Speaker two too quiet. Good visuals. Answered questions well."

Divyansh read only one line: the financial slide. That was his. He had sent it at 1 a.m. the night before.

On the walk to the canteen, Mohit tried to talk about the time overrun. Divyansh wasn't listening. We lost because of my slide. If I'd sent it on time, we'd have rehearsed, and we'd have come first.

"We ran four minutes over, and I was the speaker who was too quiet," Mohit said. "That wasn't your slide."

Divyansh shook his head. "It all started with me."

He didn't eat his samosa.

qa.q: What position did Divyansh's team come?
qa.a: Fourth out of six.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh read only the line about the financial slide?
qa.a: He already felt guilty about sending it at 1 a.m., so his attention went straight to his own part and ignored the other causes. Blaming himself felt more certain than looking at the whole sheet.

qa.q: What could help Divyansh see the result more fairly?
qa.a: Going through all six lines of feedback with the team and marking which ones were about his slide and which weren't. Seeing that most comments were about other things would show his real share.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when Divyansh ignores him admitting he was the quiet speaker?
qa.a: Mohit might feel unheard, maybe even a bit frustrated, since Mohit was trying to share the responsibility. Divyansh taking all the blame leaves no room for the team to learn together.

grounding: A student believes his team lost a competition only because of his late slide, ignoring the many other causes listed in the feedback.

subtype: Taking full blame for a group failure [Actor]
passage:
Subject: Sorry about the project

Hi Indu,

I've been meaning to write since Friday. I know you were team leader and you worked the hardest, so I owe you this.

We got a C on the urban planning project, and it's my fault. I uploaded the transport slide at 11:55, five minutes before the deadline, and I know you had to squeeze it into the file without checking it properly. That's why the whole thing looked messy.

I know the professor said the survey sample was too small, and that the model got damaged on the bus, and that Pritam's section ran long. But none of that would have mattered if the slide had been on time. It all traces back to me.

I really don't think I should be in your group next semester. You deserve someone who doesn't drag everyone down.

Sorry again.
Vaibhav

qa.q: At what time did Vaibhav upload the transport slide?
qa.a: At 11:55, five minutes before the deadline.

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav believe "it all traces back to me" even after listing other problems?
qa.a: Vaibhav's guilt about the late slide is so strong that it pulls every other cause towards Vaibhav. The email mentions the survey, the damaged model and the long section, then dismisses them.

qa.q: What would you advise Vaibhav before sending this email?
qa.a: Rewrite it to own just the late slide: apologise for it and say how to avoid it next time. Vaibhav could ask Indu to go through the other causes together instead of quitting the group.

qa.q: How might Indu, as team leader, feel reading this email?
qa.a: Indu may feel touched that Vaibhav cares but also worried about Vaibhav taking all the blame. As team leader, Indu knows the other problems too and may want to offer reassurance.

grounding: A student believes the whole group project failed because of one late slide, dismissing the survey, model and timing problems the same email lists.

subtype: Mapping the share of causes [Response]
passage:
Monday: Only four people turned up for Anand's first community drumming workshop in the Kochi town hall. He had printed thirty name tags. That night he told Disha, "I'm useless at this. It's all my fault."

Wednesday: Disha put a paper and a pencil in front of him at breakfast. "Before you decide that, draw a circle. What led to four people?" Anand grumbled, then started dividing. Posters went up late, only five days before: his part, maybe a quarter. Exam season for college students: a big slice. Heavy rain that evening: another slice. The hall being far from the bus stand: a slice. He shaded his quarter darker than the others.

Saturday: He sat with the chart and wrote next to his slice: "Posters three weeks early." Next to the rest: "Pick a date after exams. Choose the library hall near the bus stand."

He didn't feel like a failure. He felt like a person with a plan.

qa.q: How many name tags had Anand printed?
qa.a: He had printed thirty name tags.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling on Monday night, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and defeated, which shows when he tells Disha "I'm useless at this. It's all my fault." Taking all the blame made the setback feel like a verdict on him.

qa.q: Why does giving each cause a slice, including his own, help Anand?
qa.a: It lets him own his real part, the late posters, without carrying the rain, exams and hall location too. That balance turns shame into specific changes for next time.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt seeing the circle shaded and labelled on Saturday?
qa.a: Disha probably felt relieved and glad that the simple circle helped Anand move from blaming himself to planning. It shows Disha's nudge worked without lecturing.

grounding: Over several days a young man draws a pie chart of what caused a poorly attended workshop, owns his slice and no more, and turns the setback into a plan.

subtype: Mapping the share of causes [Response]
passage:
Saurabh, you've been sighing over that failed tender since Friday. Let your Mehak Maasi tell you what I did at your age.

I was twenty-four, the youngest engineer in a small firm in Nagpur, and our bid for the new bridge got rejected. I was sure it was me. I'd done the cost sheet, and I'd missed a line for steel transport.

My senior, Mr Bhosale, took a piece of chalk and drew a big circle on the site office blackboard. "What caused this? Each thing gets a slice."

We filled it together. The rival bid was fifteen percent cheaper: a huge slice. The client changed the drawings twice: another big slice. The deadline was moved up by a week: a slice. My missed line: a thin slice. Maybe one tenth.

I remember staring at that thin slice. It was mine. I owned it. But it wasn't the whole circle.

Next bid, I made a checklist for transport costs. We won that one.

qa.q: What had Mehak missed on the cost sheet?
qa.a: A line for steel transport.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when she stared at her thin slice?
qa.a: She seemed relieved and steadier, seeing that her mistake was real but only about one tenth of the cause. Owning it without carrying the whole failure gave her balance.

qa.q: Which part of Mr Bhosale's method made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Giving every cause its own slice, including hers. It kept her honest about the missed line while showing the cheaper rival bid and changed drawings mattered more, so she learned a specific lesson.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel hearing Maasi's story about the bridge bid?
qa.a: Saurabh might feel less alone and more hopeful that one failed tender doesn't define a person. The story also gives Saurabh a way to look at their own share.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, at twenty-four, she drew a pie chart of the causes of a lost bid, owned her thin slice and no more, and learned from it.
